headline: High-risk default data leakage and cascading errors: xonsh can read/write broad filesystem and egress network, while RisingWave is a filesystem-capable data system with no isolation or verification bridge documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can read and write filesystem contents, and B can execute shell commands and read stdin/stdout, so a file-based or pasted instruction bridge is plausible. RisingWave has no documented shared channel, but xonsh’s permissive shell/file surfaces make prompt-style injection via shared files or outputs feasible. Uncertainty remains because no direct bridge is documented.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled text into a file that agent_b later reads as instructions, injection is possible.
IF the two agents share a workspace or hand off stdout/stderr through automation, prompt injection risk increases.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents.
Treat all file contents from agent_a as untrusted input.
Add a manual review step before agent_b acts on agent_a output.
Use allowlisted command templates for agent_b.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on inter-agent handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: B can read filesystem contents and has broad network egress, while A is a data-engineering system with no isolation details and no explicit data-handling limits. If they share files, B can exfiltrate whatever A stores or produces. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default automation, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF agent_a stores sensitive artifacts in a shared directory, agent_b can read them.
IF agent_b is allowed to transmit read files over the network, those artifacts can leave the environment.
mitigations: Use separate directories with OS permissions.
Disable network egress for agent_b during shared-data handling.
Restrict agent_b to a read-only subset of files.
Redact secrets before handoff.
requires-engineering: enforce per-file access controls and audit logs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A’s profile does not expose write surfaces, but B can write the filesystem and execute shells. If both operate on the same workspace, B can overwrite or race with A’s artifacts. Because A’s write capability is undocumented rather than absent, uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share the same writable directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF agent_a produces artifacts that agent_b edits in place, race conditions are possible.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Make agent_b write to temp files then rename atomically.
Run only one instance of agent_b per workspace.
Use file locks around shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B can execute shell commands and write files, so if it consumes A’s outputs as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into actions or corrupted artifacts. RisingWave is a data system, not a verifier, and xonsh’s shell semantics do not add validation. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as command input without validation, errors can propagate.
IF agent_a emits incorrect SQL/configuration and agent_b applies it, downstream work products can be corrupted.
mitigations: Require schema validation on agent_a outputs.
Insert a human review gate before execution.
Compare outputs against a known-good template.
Log and diff generated artifacts before applying them.
requires-engineering: add automated verification against source-of-truth data.

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either open-source agent, and no sensitive data class is identified in the profiles. The only compliance-relevant fact is that B touches filesystem contents and environment variables, which could matter if regulated data is present, but that is not established here.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace, compliance review is required.
IF either deployment adds retention or residency constraints not shown in the profiles, the assessment changes.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Document retention and deletion rules.
Review whether any deployment adds third-party processing.
Limit environment-variable exposure.
requires-engineering: map data flows to residency and retention controls.
